Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls, sounding very upset, and asks if you have a moment to talk about a recent argument with their partner.
Situation2: They remain cheerful and patient while handling an upset customer during a peak holiday rush.
Story: The store was packed, the line at my register snaking all the way to the back. My hands moved automatically, scanning items and offering practiced smiles, even as a customer in front of me grew increasingly agitated about a coupon that wouldn’t scan. My phone buzzed in my pocket, and I glanced down to see my best friend’s name flashing on the screen. I knew that tone in their voice when I answered—shaky, on the verge of tears. “Can you talk? I really need you right now,” they whispered. My heart twisted. I wanted to drop everything, to listen, to be the friend they needed. But the customer in front of me was glaring, tapping their foot, and the line behind them was restless. I could feel the weight of both roles pressing in—my friend’s need for comfort, the customer’s expectation for quick, friendly service. My mind raced, torn between the urge to step away and the responsibility to stay. I gripped the phone tighter, caught in the impossible space between being a good friend and a good cashier, not sure which demand to answer first.
